newsitem.title: USA: Fitch cuts Hartford, Conn., GO bonds to AA-minus.
newsitem.headline: Fitch cuts Hartford, Conn., GO bonds to AA-minus.

text.p: Hartford, CT.'s $25,000,000 general obligation bonds (GO), for competitive bids Dec. 5, are rated 'AA-' by Fitch Investors Service.
The rating on the outstanding and currently offered GO bonds has been lowered to 'AA-' from 'AA', reflecting the long-term losses in the tax and employment bases.
Although the magnitude of deterioration appears to be decelerating, assessment and employment declines continue to be evidenced.

Offsetting factors include the low debt burden and continued strong finances and financial management. Also, with this rating action, the negative outlook is removed. The new issue bonds will mature serially Dec. 15, 1997-2016 and be optionally callable beginning Dec. 15, 2006 at 102%. Hartford remains a city of two characters.

The substantial tax base is composed primarily of commercial/industrial property. The residents are less well off than their suburban neighbors and service requirements, particularily for education, are high. Excellent management, through tight financial controls, continues to maintain financial position with solid balances. Unaudited results for fiscal 1996 show an unreserved balance of $27.7 million, equal to 6.5% of current revenues.

Operational issues remain problematic in the city-funded school system -- both the city, within its limited legal authority, and the state are increasingly engaged in efforts to address them. Notwithstanding its long record of strong financial management, Hartford faces ongoing pressures, potentially exacerbated by continuing weakness in multiple economic indicators.

Hartford's recovery continues to lag the state's, which in turn is lagging the nation's. The unemployment rate remains high and assessed value continues to decline, albeit at a slower rate and by lesser amounts.
While various insurance and financial services corporations have continued to downsize, other corporations and service providers have announced intentions to relocate to Hartford.

In conjunction with the private sector, abutting towns and the state and federal governments, the city continues to actively pursue a number of economic development initiatives. Moreover, several large corporations have reaffirmed their commitments to remain in the city. It is premature to determine whether these efforts will stabilize the economy.
